rv.q: What is acutely shown, though, is how the sisters refuse to be passive victims, sometimes colluding with the family’s plans, at other times attempting to assert their own will.
This is a very classy production indeed, which must surely live beyond its Chichester summer.

Poulton’s decision to leave the three Boleyn siblings still naively plotting for their future, unaware that for two of them, execution dates were being set and axes sharpened, is a tense and chilling end note to an irresistible take on this hushed-up slice of history.
It makes for a full-bodied and really enjoyable evening and will do nothing to reduce the fascination that we still have with the Tudors.

The piece, in all its power, is performed by a generally strong cast of eighteen with especially noteworthy work from Lucy Phelps as Mary, troubled, determined, put-upon and wanting nothing more than to be allowed to retire to Kent with her children.
However, it is an unquestionably beautiful production which is well executed and will be enjoyed by fans of the genre.
Chichester Festival Theatre have produced a strong opener to their new season, and this has set the bar high for what is to follow.

cn.t: Critics praise this sumptuous adaptation of Philippa Gregory's bestseller, calling it a tense and compelling crowd-pleaser that brings the conniving Boleyn family sharply to life with robust performances and chilling drama.
